# Modern C++ for Performance: RAII, Move Semantics, Stack Allocation Last verified: 2026-10-30 against cppreference.com (std::move, move_if_noexcept, vector::push_back and reserve, unique_ptr::release, lock_guard, copy elision) and Apple's `xctrace` help output on this Mac; the demos were compiled with Apple clang 17 (`-std=c++20 -O2`) and run on an Apple M4 Mac. Latency numbers in the old draft were invented and have been removed; this lesson quotes none. Starts from: basic C++ (classes, constructors, `new`/`delete`, `std::vector`). ## Overview Low-latency systems (trading engines, inference servers) care about how long one request takes in the worst case, not only on average. "P99" means the 99th percentile: 99% of requests are faster than that value. C++ gives you tools that make cost visible: 1. **RAII** (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization): an object acquires a resource in its constructor and releases it in its destructor, so cleanup happens at a known point. 2. **Move semantics**: transfer a resource from one object to another instead of duplicating it. 3. **Stack allocation**: local objects need no call to the allocator. 4. **Smart pointers**: `std::unique_ptr` and friends are RAII for heap memory. This lesson is the mental model, not syntax drills. Measuring is lesson 03's job and the last section here. --- ## RAII: ownership and determinism A destructor runs when an object's scope ends, on every path out of it: normal return, early return, or exception. ```cpp void process_order(const Order& o) { Buffer buf(1024); // ctor acquires if (o.is_valid()) { /* use buf */ } } // dtor releases, even if an exception flew ``` The manual alternative, `Buffer* buf = new Buffer(1024); ... delete buf;`, leaks on any path that skips the `delete`. Demo (`raii_move.cpp`, compiled and run): a `Buffer` that prints in its constructor and destructor, used by a function that either finishes or throws. ``` Buffer: acquire work: finished normally Buffer: release Buffer: acquire Buffer: release caught: boom ``` The destructor ran in both cases, before the `catch` block saw the exception. Standard-library RAII types: `std::lock_guard` ("provides a convenient RAII-style mechanism for owning a mutex for the duration of a scoped block", cppreference), `std::unique_ptr`, `std::vector`. ```cpp { std::lock_guard lock(mutex_); // locks // critical section } // unlocks here auto o = std::make_unique(/*...*/); // freed when o goes out of scope ``` **Is RAII free?** Usually cheap, not guaranteed free: a destructor is real code, and compilers often inline small ones. Do not say "zero cost" in an interview; say "no cost beyond the cleanup you would have written by hand". **Interview angle:** "Why is RAII better than try/finally?" C++ has no `finally`. Languages that do make cleanup something each caller must remember to write; with RAII the cleanup is attached to the type, so callers cannot forget it. --- ## Move semantics and perfect forwarding Two terms first. An **lvalue** is an expression that names an object you can refer to again (`order`). An **rvalue** is a temporary or something you have marked as expendable (`Order{...}` or `std::move(order)`). A reference to an rvalue is written `T&&`. Copying a large object duplicates its resources. Moving lets the destination take the resources from the source. ```cpp orders.push_back(large_order); // overload taking const T&: copy orders.push_back(std::move(large_order)); // overload taking T&&: move ``` `push_back` has both overloads: "1) The new element is initialized as a copy of value. 2) value is moved into the new element." (cppreference). **`std::move` does not move anything.** cppreference: it "produces an xvalue expression that identifies its argument", "exactly equivalent to a static_cast to an rvalue reference type". It only lets the compiler pick the move overload. Whether anything is cheaper depends on what the type's move constructor does. ```mermaid graph LR A["obj1
owns buffer"] -->|"move ctor"| C["obj2
owns buffer"] A -->|"leaves"| D["obj1
valid but
unspecified"] ``` Three special members: ```cpp Order(const Order& other); // copy constructor Order(Order&& other) noexcept; // move constructor Order& operator=(Order&& other) noexcept; // move assignment ``` **A move is only cheap if the type owns something to hand over.** An `Order` that is a plain struct with `char data[128]` has no pointer to steal, so its "move" is a copy of 128 bytes. A `std::string` or `std::vector` member does have one. Check before claiming a speed-up. **Mark move operations `noexcept`.** When a `std::vector` grows it must relocate its elements. cppreference (`move_if_noexcept`): the vector uses it "to decide whether to use move construction or copy construction" so that an exception during growth can be undone. Demo (`nothrow.cpp`, compiled and run), growing a vector of a type whose move constructor is not `noexcept` versus one that is: ``` A grow: copy B grow: move ``` Type `A` (move constructor not `noexcept`) was copied on reallocation; type `B` (`noexcept`) was moved. Apple clang 17 with libc++, as of 2026-10-30; the rule is standard-library behaviour, but the exact output depends on the implementation. **After a move the source is valid but unspecified.** cppreference: "all standard library objects that have been moved from are placed in a 'valid but unspecified state'". You may destroy it, assign to it, or call functions that have no preconditions (`clear()`, `empty()`). Using it is *not* undefined behavior; relying on its contents is a bug. In the demo a moved-from `std::string` happened to have size 0, which the standard does not promise. **Returning a local needs no `std::move`.** `return v;` can construct `v` directly in the caller (copy elision, "NRVO"), which is allowed but not mandatory; if it is not done, the compiler tries the move constructor. Writing `return std::move(v);` can block the elision. Demo (`nrvo.cpp`): returning a local `std::vector` printed neither "copy" nor "move". **Perfect forwarding** passes an argument on keeping its value category (lvalue stays lvalue, rvalue stays rvalue): ```cpp template void store(T&& obj) { // forwarding reference container.push_back(std::forward(obj)); } Order o; store(o); // lvalue: push_back copies store(Order{}); // rvalue: push_back moves ``` `T&&` on a deduced template parameter is a *forwarding reference*, not a plain rvalue reference. **Interview angle:** "When do you use `std::move`?" Answer: when you are done with an object and want to hand its resources to someone else. After that, treat it as empty: assign to it or destroy it. It is not undefined behaviour to use it, but its value is unspecified. --- ## Stack allocation and cache locality A local variable (`Order o;`) lives in the function's stack frame; creating it needs no call to the allocator. `new Order()` asks the allocator for memory and gives you a pointer you must follow, which usually means touching another cache line. A **cache line** is the unit the CPU moves between memory and cache (commonly 64 bytes on x86). Caches are small, fast memories between the CPU and main memory, in levels (L1 smallest and fastest, then L2, L3). Data you touched recently or sit next to something you touched is likely already there. This machine's numbers, from `sysctl hw.cachelinesize hw.l1dcachesize hw.l2cachesize` on an Apple M4 (Mac16,1), as of 2026-10-30: ``` hw.cachelinesize: 128 hw.l1dcachesize: 65536 hw.l2cachesize: 4194304 ``` So the cache line here is 128 bytes, not the 64 you will see quoted for x86. Other CPUs differ; look yours up instead of memorizing one figure. Latency numbers per level are not given here because this lesson has no captured measurement for them. ```mermaid graph TD A["Main memory
biggest, slowest"] --> B["L3 / system cache"] B --> C["L2"] C --> D["L1
smallest, fastest"] D --> E["Registers"] ``` **What stays on the stack and what does not.** `std::vector fills;` puts only the small vector object (a few pointers) on the stack; the elements live on the heap, obtained from the allocator. `fills.reserve(100)` makes that one allocation up front, so later `push_back`s do not reallocate and "insertions will not trigger reallocation unless the insertion would make the size of the vector greater than the value of capacity()" (cppreference). Reserving is orthogonal to moving: one avoids reallocation, the other avoids copying. ```cpp void match_order(const Order& buy, const Order& sell) { std::vector fills; fills.reserve(100); // one heap allocation for (int i = 0; i < buy.qty; ++i) fills.push_back({buy.id, sell.id, 1}); } // dtor frees the buffer ``` **Rule of thumb (the author's heuristic, not a standard):** keep small objects of known size on the stack; put large, variable-sized, or long-lived data on the heap. The stack is limited: `ulimit -s` printed 8176 (KB) in a macOS shell here, and other threads and platforms use other sizes, so do not put big arrays in locals. --- ## Profiling: how to prove a performance claim Measure before and after, on the same machine, and name the machine. **perf (Linux only; not run on macOS for this lesson).** `perf record -F 99 -g ./app` samples at 99 Hz (`-F`: "Profile at this frequency"; `-g`: "Enables call-graph (stack chain/backtrace) recording for both kernel space and user space", man7 perf-record page). `perf report` then shows where samples landed. **Flame graphs.** On Linux, Brendan Gregg's FlameGraph scripts turn perf stacks into an SVG. How to read one (brendangregg.com/flamegraphs.html): "the y-axis shows stack depth", "the x-axis shows the stack profile population, sorted alphabetically (it is not the passage of time)", "the wider a frame is, the more often it was present in the stacks." So look for wide frames, not tall ones. **macOS.** The old `instruments` command is not installed on this Mac; the command-line tool is `xctrace`. `xcrun xctrace list templates` here includes `Time Profiler`, `System Trace`, `Allocations` and `Leaks`, and its help shows `xctrace record --template 'Time Profiler' --all-processes --time-limit 5s`. **Measurement strategy (author's practice):** record long enough to cover steady state rather than startup; look at the top few functions by samples; change one thing; re-measure. **Interview trap:** "It is fast because I use smart pointers." That is a claim about performance, and only a measurement can support it. --- ## Q&A **Recall 1:** Explain RAII in one sentence. Why is it better than manual cleanup? *Must-say:* - An object's constructor acquires a resource and its destructor releases it, so cleanup runs on every exit path including exceptions. - The caller cannot forget it; manual cleanup depends on every path remembering. **Probe 1:** You have `std::unique_ptr o` and a function `void process(Order* p)`. What happens with `process(o.get())` and with `process(o.release())`? *Expected:* - `get()` hands out the raw pointer; `o` still owns the object and frees it at scope end. `process` must not delete it. - `release()` gives up ownership: cppreference says "The caller is responsible for cleaning up the object". If `process` does not delete it, it leaks. **Probe 2:** A vector of `Order` where `Order` has a deleted copy constructor and a move constructor. What happens with `push_back(order)` and with `push_back(std::move(order))`? *Expected:* - With an lvalue the copy overload needs CopyInsertable, so it does not compile. - With `std::move` the `T&&` overload is chosen and the move constructor runs. **Numeric 1 (hypothetical numbers):** Assume a heap allocation plus free costs 200 ns in your allocator, and a function does it once per call and is called 1,000,000 times per second. What fraction of one core does that use, and what does reusing a buffer change? *Working:* 200 ns x 1,000,000 = 0.2 s per second, so 20% of one core on allocator calls alone. Reusing a preallocated buffer removes those calls. The 200 ns is an assumption in the question, not a measured figure; measure your allocator. **Numeric 2 (hypothetical numbers):** A loop reads 1,000 `Order` objects of 128 bytes each. How much memory is that, and which caches could hold it on a CPU with a 32 KB L1 and 256 KB L2? *Working:* 1,000 x 128 B = 128,000 B, about 125 KB. It does not fit in 32 KB L1, but it does fit in a 256 KB L2, so after the first pass most reads can hit L2, not main memory. Whether they are contiguous matters too: a `std::vector` is contiguous, a list of separately allocated orders is not. --- ## Questions for the Interviewer - How does your team profile performance (perf, custom instrumentation, flame graphs)? - Do you use preallocation or object pools in latency-sensitive code? - How do you review move constructors, for example whether they are `noexcept`? - Have you hit RAII gotchas (exceptions thrown from destructors, ownership confusion)? ## Sources - https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/utility/move : what `std::move` does; "valid but unspecified state". - https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/utility/move_if_noexcept : vector growth uses move only if the move constructor is `noexcept` (or the type is move-only). - https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector/push_back : copy and move overloads and their requirements. - https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/container/vector/reserve : reserve allocates new storage via the allocator; later insertions do not reallocate within capacity. - https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/memory/unique_ptr/release : `release()` and the caller's responsibility. - https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/thread/lock_guard : RAII mutex ownership. - https://en.cppreference.com/w/cpp/language/copy_elision : NRVO is allowed, not mandatory; implicit move on return. - https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/perf-record.1.html : `-F` and `-g`. - https://www.brendangregg.com/flamegraphs.html : how to read a flame graph. - Local: `xcrun xctrace help` and `xcrun xctrace list templates`, `sysctl hw.*cachesize`, `ulimit -s` on an Apple M4 Mac, 2026-10-30.
